summary: Defines management objects for monitoring DNS name server functions. It was produced by the DNS working group. It is historic.

eli5.summary: Gauges that let an administrator watch how a DNS server, the Internet's phone-book helper, is doing.

questions: how to monitor a dns name server with snmp
subtitle: Gauges and controls that let system administrators watch and manage how a DNS server is performing.

tldr.problem: DNS name servers are critical infrastructure, but system administrators had no standard way to monitor their health, performance, and configuration using SNMP (the standard network management protocol).
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a set of managed objects (the MIB) that expose DNS server configuration, statistics, and zone information to SNMP management stations. The objects are organized into four groups: server configuration, server counters, optional counters (by query source), and zone management.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can now monitor DNS server uptime, query response statistics, error rates, and zone reloads through standard SNMP tools, enabling integrated management of DNS with the rest of the network. This RFC is Historic.

facts.label: Configuration objects
facts.value: 5 (implementation, recursion, uptime, reset time, reset control)

facts.label: Counter categories
facts.value: Authoritative, cached, no-such-name, referrals, errors, unparseable

today: RFC 1611 is a Historic protocol. While modern DNS server implementations still exist, SNMP-based management has declined in favor of web-based dashboards and cloud-native observability tools. However, the MIB structures defined here influenced later DNS and SNMP work, and the document remains a useful reference for understanding DNS server instrumentation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is critical infrastructure for any IP network, translating names like example.com into addresses. Like any critical service, DNS servers need monitoring and management.

This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for DNS name servers, enabling their monitoring and configuration through SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol). Before this, administrators had no standard way to observe DNS server performance or control its behavior from a central management station.

The MIB defines managed objects in four groups: configuration objects (software version, recursion mode, uptime), counters for query types and responses, optional counters for query sources (local, trusted, or remote), and zone management (zone loading and synchronization).
sections.eli5: DNS servers need to be watched and controlled. This is the standard way to peek at what a DNS server is doing and adjust its settings using SNMP, which is how network gear talks to management computers.

sections.title: DNS Resolvers and Servers
sections.content:
The DNS world has two main types of entities: resolvers and name servers. A resolver asks questions (queries) for domain names and receives answers. A name server receives queries and sends answers.

A full resolver is sophisticated, knowing how to find the authoritative name server for any name. A stub resolver is simpler, just sending all queries to a configured local name server with a flag meaning please resolve this for me. A resolver may cache answers to speed up future queries.

A name server serves resource records to resolvers. It receives queries and sends replies but does not send queries or cache data. An authoritative name server has the official record for a domain. If a name server receives a query it cannot answer authoritatively, it may ask a resolver within itself to look up the answer.

The MIB in this RFC covers only name server functions. A separate MIB (the DNS Resolver MIB) covers resolvers. A DNS entity performing both roles would implement both MIBs.
sections.eli5: Resolvers are question-askers, name servers are answer-givers. Some programs do both. This document describes how to watch the name-server part with SNMP.

sections.title: MIB Groups and Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The MIB defines objects in four functional groups.

The Server Configuration Group includes the software implementation identifier, recursion availability (whether the server performs recursive queries), uptime, and time since last reset or configuration reload.

The Server Counter Group provides global statistics: counts of authoritative answers, non-authoritative (cached) answers, no-such-name responses, referrals to other servers, error responses, and unparseable requests. A counter table breaks down counts by query opcode, class, type, and transport (UDP or TCP).

The Server Optional Counter Group further breaks down responses by their source: queries from the local host (the server itself), queries from trusted friends (typically an access list), and queries from remote untrusted hosts. This lets administrators see if the server is answering mostly for itself, for trusted clients, or for the wider Internet.

The Server Zone Group tracks zones that the server loads and serves authoritatively, including zone serial numbers, last successful reload times, and the IP addresses of source servers for zone transfers.

Several textual conventions represent DNS data types (DnsName, DnsClass, DnsType, DnsOpCode, DnsRespCode) as non-enumerated integers, allowing the MIB to accommodate future DNS extensions without change.
sections.eli5: Four categories of information: how the server is set up, how many queries it got and answered, who asked the questions, and what zones it serves. The definitions use extensible type numbers so DNS can add new types later.

sections.title: Configuration and Control
sections.content:
The configuration group exposes server behavior that administrators may want to observe or change.

The recursion control object indicates whether the server performs recursive lookups (available), whether it restricts recursion to certain clients only (restricted), or does not perform recursion at all (unavailable). An administrator can read or write this to adjust what the server will do for different clients.

The uptime object reports seconds elapsed since the server started (or zero if stateless). The reset-time object reports seconds since the last configuration reload or restart.

The reset object allows an administrator to issue a reset command, causing the server to re-read its configuration files and restart its process. Reading this object returns the server's current state: other (unknown), initializing, or running. Writing reset(2) triggers the restart.
sections.eli5: An administrator can see if the server handles recursive queries, how long it has been running, and can tell it to restart and re-read its configuration.

sections.title: Monitoring and Zone Management
sections.content:
The counter objects provide visibility into DNS server load and behavior. Global counts track how many queries resulted in authoritative answers, cached answers, referrals, and errors. The counter table allows drill-down by query type (A record for addresses, MX for mail servers, etc.) and transport (UDP vs. TCP).

The optional counter group shows where queries originate. If most queries are local (from the server's own resolver), the server is providing recursive service. If many come from friends (access-list members), it serves a trusted community. If many are remote, the server carries significant transit traffic.

The zone table lists zones that the server loads and serves. For each zone, the MIB tracks the serial number (from the SOA record), whether the zone is currently valid, and timestamps for reload attempts and successes. The zone-source table lists IP addresses of secondary servers from which this server may pull zone transfers. An administrator uses this to manage zone replication and watch for transfer failures.
sections.eli5: See how many queries came in, what kind they were, who asked, and whether the zone files are up to date and valid.

sections.title: Management and Compliance
sections.content:
The MIB is organized as SNMPv2 object groups and compliance statements. Mandatory groups are the configuration group and counter group; every name server MIB must implement these. The optional counter group is unconditionally optional; servers may omit it. The zone group is mandatory only for authoritative servers that load zones.

Some objects are read-only (uptime, counters), while others are read-write to allow management (recursion setting, reset command). The specification notes that the recursion and reset objects need not be writable in some implementations.

The RFC defers to the SNMP framework for security, authentication, and access control. Security is handled by SNMP authentication and community access lists, not by the MIB itself.
sections.eli5: The MIB is organized into required and optional parts. Some settings can be changed from SNMP, others are read-only. SNMP itself handles security and who is allowed to look or change things.
